extracted.intended_audience: authors submitting papers for peer review (especially graduate students), for both conferences and journals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, stepwise guidance for composing rebuttals to peer reviews for journal and conference submissions: formatting, tone, content, prioritization, and post-rebuttal revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective of a rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective in a rebuttal is to convey confidence to reviewers: We acknowledge your criticism and advice; we understand your misunderstanding; and we can fully integrate this feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the rebuttal so reviewers feel heard, show you understand their points, and demonstrate that you can and will integrate feedback. This is the high-level goal that should shape tone and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be polite
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not lash out at a negative reviewer; hostile language won't change opinions. Maintain courteous language throughout the rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be conciliatory
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reviewer is wrong, don't say they're wrong. Use phrasing such as "there seems to be a misunderstanding." If the misunderstanding arose from poor presentation, admit it and offer to fix it. Avoid confrontational framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be thorough
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reply to every point, minor or large. Don't dodge points or refuse to answer questions. If reviewers found a flaw, admit it and offer a fix (if you can find one). Thoroughness includes addressing both factual objections and presentation misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish journal vs conference rebuttals
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of rebuttals: journal-submission rebuttals and conference-submission rebuttals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal rebuttals: typically allowed when work is acceptable but needs revision; you often have a few weeks, are expected to produce a new version, can cite changes, and may have multiple review rounds until objections are satisfied. Conference rebuttals: may be length-limited (500–1000 words), have only 2–3 days to respond, and may be the only chance to respond before final judgment. Tweak the same process to fit constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Indent (quote reviews verbatim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you've received your reviews, put them all in a file, and indent the whole file with >.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the reviewers' text verbatim with quotation marks or > prefixes (and reviewer labels like "-- Reviewer 1 --"). This makes it explicit what you're replying to and preserves context for each quoted point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2: Reply to all points (inline responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Next, reply to every point of all reviews, minor or large, as you would in a traditional academic email.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond inline after each quoted point. For summaries, indicate accuracy or missing details. For claims (e.g., novelty, triviality, correctness), either acknowledge, provide distinguishing evidence or clarify misunderstandings. Use specific examples, refer to sections/pages in the paper, and present cases that highlight distinctions from prior work. Example patterns in the text: agree where appropriate, show counterexamples/cases when contesting prior-work claims, explain when the presentation caused confusion, and offer fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete evidence and pointer to paper changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When contesting reviewer claims, provide concrete distinctions and point to where in the paper you discussed or will discuss them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., when a reviewer says X is not novel, explain how your method generalizes prior work, give a motivating case beyond prior limits, and cite the related-work location (page number). When admitting a presentation flaw, explain how you'll fix it in the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone for disagreement: attribute to misunderstanding/presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reviewer finds something incorrect, prefer attributing it to a misunderstanding or presentation issue rather than calling the reviewer wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase things like "It appears that there is a misunderstanding" and clarify what the reviewer seems to have taken away (e.g., reviewer thinks Z is Z') and why that led to the error. This keeps the tone conciliatory while correcting substantive errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 3: Sort replies by importance
rubrics_metrics.description: If submitting to a conference, make sure the most important points are at the top. Sort all of your replies in order of importance, point by point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because conference reviewers/PC may skim, place the most persuasive, high-impact rebuttals first. Reorder your inline replies so that the top of the document contains the reviewer-written summaries you want to affirm and the most critical clarifications or fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 4: Cut for length and redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: If your reply is limited in length or replies are redundant between reviewers, trim your response, starting at the bottom (least important points) and working up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove low-priority or duplicated replies to meet word limits. Keep stronger, higher-priority points near the top; trim details and peripheral clarifications last.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 5: Polish — highlight accurate reviewer summaries and thank reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Push the most accurate reviewer-written summary of your work to the top of your rebuttal to confirm this point of view. Add a "thank you" to the top of the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amplify reviewer summaries that correctly capture your contribution (e.g., "This is an accurate summary, and we'd like to amplify recognition of W"). Since some committee members may only glance, put a brief, precise summary and gratitude at the top. Try to place yourself in the reviewer's mind and ask whether you'd be satisfied with the answers if you were them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reviewer-provided summaries strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reviewer provides an accurate high-level summary, quote it near the top and confirm/clarify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps quickly convey the main contributions to committee members who may not have read the full paper. Explicitly comment to make it precise and, if useful, note additional contributions (e.g., W) identified by another reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge time and effort of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Thank the reviewers for the time and expertise they have invested in these reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a polite thank-you in the rebuttal. Recognize reviewing as a service; this contributes to a congenial tone and may predispose readers favorably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 6: Relax and revise (post-rebuttal work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once your rebuttal is in, relax. Then, spend time incorporating the reviewer's feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After submitting the rebuttal, immediately start incorporating changes into the manuscript to produce a stronger final version or a better resubmission. The rebuttal is only part of the process; follow-through matters.
